title: Agentic Workflows on Vertex AI: Rukma Sen

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core focus is defining agent architectures, contrasting single-agent vs multi-agent patterns with dispatcher, expert, and supervisor roles. Use cases span general-purpose agent patterns while Vertex AI and Agent Builder are developer-platform infrastructure. The talk covers agent design patterns and building agents on Vertex AI's platform. summary: Rukma Sen, representing Google Cloud's Vertex AI team, frames agents as the defining interface for human-AI interaction, comparing the shift to how the internet changed human-technology interaction from physical appliances to screen-based gestures. She stresses that developers building agents carry responsibility for safety, ethics, cybersecurity, data privacy, and preventing misinformation, especially as wearables and unobtrusive compute proliferate. She offers a working definition: an AI agent is a system designed to achieve specific goals by interacting with its environment. Three core components form every agent: the model (the brain, responsible for reasoning, planning, and guiding behavior), tools (the hands, enabling actions like fetching data or calling external APIs), and orchestration (the nervous system, maintaining memory and state). She distinguishes three agent types: deterministic agents follow fixed rules and always return consistent outputs (e.g., a calculator); generative agents produce diverse, creative outputs (e.g., a customer service chatbot); and hybrid agents combine both (e.g., a financial advisor using deterministic analysis with generative communication). On architecture, she contrasts single-agent systems—where one model handles reasoning, planning, and acting—with multi-agent architectures. Single agents can fail on simple tasks; she illustrates this with a prompt asking the model to count the letter A in banana, where the model gives inconsistent answers. Multi-agent systems assign specialized roles: a dispatcher agent triages incoming issues, subject-matter expert agents handle specific domains, and a supervisor agent quality-checks outputs. She shares an anecdote where her supervisor agent repeatedly rejected outputs until she rebuilt the system. She then surveys use cases across customer support, e-commerce, B2B, and travel, adding internal-facing employee agents for HR tasks like enrollment and benefits, knowledge agents specialized in domains like legal, and voice agents for multimodal scenarios such as fast food drive-thrus where the agent transcribes spoken orders and sends them to the ordering system. She closes by highlighting Vertex AI as a full-lifecycle AI development platform offering 150-plus models including Google first-party, Anthropic, Llama 2 and 3, and open-source models, with Model Garden for model selection and fine-tuning, and Agent Builder for no-code to high-code agent construction, all backed by Google Cloud enterprise security and compute orchestration. She emphasizes the platform is built developer-first and invites feedback.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Agent Interface
sections.summary: Rukma introduces herself and frames agents as the primary interface between generative AI and users, comparing the shift to the internet's impact on human-technology interaction.

sections.title: Responsibility and Ethics
sections.summary: Discusses ethical considerations, safety, cybersecurity, and data privacy responsibilities developers carry when building agents.

sections.title: What is an AI Agent
sections.summary: Defines AI agents as goal-achieving systems with model (brain), tools (hands), and orchestration (nervous system) components.

sections.title: Types of AI Agents
sections.summary: Covers deterministic, generative, and hybrid agents with examples like calculators, chatbots, and financial advisors.

sections.title: Single vs Multi-Agent Architecture
sections.summary: Contrasts single-agent limitations with multi-agent architectures using dispatcher, expert, and supervisor roles, including a supervisor rejection loop anecdote.

sections.title: Agent Use Cases
sections.summary: Surveys use cases across customer support, e-commerce, B2B, and travel, then extends to internal-facing employee agents for HR tasks like enrollment and benefits, knowledge agents specialized in domains such as legal, and multimodal voice agents for scenarios like fast food drive-thrus.

sections.title: Vertex AI Platform and Tooling
sections.summary: Recaps the talk's structure, then introduces Vertex AI as a full-lifecycle AI development platform offering 150+ models (Google first-party, Anthropic, Llama 2/3, open source), low-code to high-code options, Model Garden for model selection and fine-tuning, Agent Builder for agent construction, and Google Cloud enterprise security and compute orchestration.

sections.title: Closing and Call to Action
sections.summary: Emphasizes Vertex AI is built developer-first, invites feedback at the Google booth, and asks attendees to complete a survey in exchange for a branded water bottle.
